name: Pythagoras of Samos
note: Pythagoras holds a careful place in the hall; the right triangle's long history deserves Babylonian tablets and the Chinese gougu tradition beside his name.

name: Fibonacci of Pisa
note: Fibonacci sits in the seed lineage; his book carried Indian and Arabic arithmetic through a world that needed it.

name: Johannes Kepler
note: Kepler's measured ellipses open the sky here; patient observation became strong enough to move a planet.

name: Isaac Newton
note: Beside Kepler's ellipses stands Newton's law, because his synthesis made the sky answer to the same gravity as the earth.

name: Thomas Bayes
note: I placed Bayes at the first turn of belief; his quiet essay gave uncertainty a way to learn from evidence.

name: Leonhard Euler
note: Euler's identity rests in the spiral; his fearless fluency made five constants sound like one note.

name: Jean le Rond d'Alembert
note: At the plucked string stands d'Alembert, whose equation let a moving disturbance keep its own shape.

name: Richard Price
note: Price keeps his place beside Bayes; his editorial care carried the essay into print and made its argument reach us.

name: Pierre-Simon Laplace
note: Laplace followed the tide; he carried celestial mechanics' rigor into the breathing ocean.

name: Paolo Ruffini
note: Ruffini settles the quintic question; the missing radical formula was a mathematical fact, not a gap to fill.

name: Joseph Fourier
note: Fourier gave the ear its mathematics; his heat equation turned complex shapes into a chorus of simple waves.

name: Carl Friedrich Gauss
note: Gauss opens the surface chapter; intrinsic curvature let geometry learn to measure itself.

name: Claude-Louis Navier
note: Navier stands at the moving water; he dared to give viscosity a mathematical voice.

name: Michael Faraday
note: Faraday's field lines hold their own light beside Maxwell; the experimental imagination came before the equations.

name: Niels Henrik Abel
note: Abel's impossibility proof stands beside Ruffini; it gave the quintic's refusal its lasting form.

name: George Gabriel Stokes
note: Stokes extends the fluid line beside Navier; his work turned a working model into a lasting law.

name: Pierre Ossian Bonnet
note: Bonnet earns the theorem's other name; his boundary term completes the conversation Gauss began.

name: Bernhard Riemann
note: I keep Riemann at the still-open line; his daring zeta function joined primes to the deep shape of analysis.

name: James Clerk Maxwell
note: Maxwell belongs among the fields; his synthesis let electricity and magnetism travel as light.

name: Ludwig Boltzmann
note: Boltzmann's logarithm stands beside entropy; he gave the invisible multitude of molecular states a measure.

name: Henri Poincaré
note: Poincaré holds the point where celestial mechanics met a limit: his nonintegrability result forbids a general integral, not the special periodic dances found later.

name: Max Planck
note: Planck's reluctant quantum sits at the century's hinge; one careful mathematical rescue opened a new physics.

name: Vito Volterra
note: Volterra works beside Lotka; his model made ecological conflict move in equations and in real fisheries.

name: Wilhelm Weinberg
note: Weinberg shares the origin beside Hardy; his independent insight gave the equilibrium a second, equally deserved origin.

name: Jacques Hadamard
note: Hadamard stands at the prime number theorem; his 1896 zero-free argument made prime density yield to complex analysis.

name: Charles-Jean de la Vallée Poussin
note: De la Vallée Poussin reached the same landmark by a second route, beside Hadamard.

name: Godfrey Harold Hardy
note: Hardy holds the inheritance balance; his algebra made a useful law visible, even beyond the field he loved.

name: James Jeans
note: Jeans's stability criterion rests near the cold cloud, where the contest between sound-crossing time and gravitational collapse becomes a mass scale.

name: Alfred Lotka
note: Lotka keeps the predator-prey rhythm; he saw a mathematical ecology in chemistry's changing concentrations.

name: Arthur Eddington
note: Eddington holds the balance between radiation and gravity, with the assumptions about opacity left visible on the page.

name: Emmy Noether
note: Noether's theorem takes the center; symmetry and conservation deserve one.

name: Erwin Schrödinger
note: Schrödinger's equation gave quantum change a form the imagination could follow.

name: Edwin Hubble
note: Hubble's careful measures stand beside Lemaître's theory; he made expansion visible, and the shared history deserves both names.

name: Georges Lemaître
note: I set Lemaître beside the expanding universe; his 1927 derivation deserves to be read before the name the world learned later.

name: Fritz Zwicky
note: Zwicky's 1933 Coma-cluster discrepancy predates the later rotation curves it sits beside; unseen mass entered astronomy before the spiral galaxies made the case vivid.

name: Werner Heisenberg
note: Heisenberg's limit is written into the structure of states; he turned a measurement boundary into a law, not a flaw.

name: Kurt Gödel
note: Gödel stands at the continuum's boundary; the constructible universe showed that one direction could not be refuted from ZFC.

name: Alan Turing
note: Turing's final work showed how reaction and diffusion can make form.

name: Alan Hodgkin
note: Hodgkin's patient measurements at the axon let nerve signals become a mechanism we can read.

name: Claude Shannon
note: Shannon's bit sits beside surprise; he made information measurable without asking what a message means.

name: Andrew Huxley
note: Huxley's gating model completes those measurements; he turned a living membrane into a working mathematical instrument.

name: Edward Lorenz
note: Lorenz stayed with the weather; his spare equations made sensitive dependence impossible to ignore.

name: Vera Rubin
note: Rubin's careful galaxy rotations hold the center of the dark-matter story; the Nobel Prize did not follow the work that changed the field.

name: Wolfgang Haken
note: Haken works beside Appel; his structural insight helped turn the four-color question into a finite check.

name: Kenneth Appel
note: Appel and Haken share the four-color page, where the computer became a visible mathematical witness.

name: Martin Vogel
note: Vogel's spacing rule runs among the seeds; he gave a striking botanical pattern a clear mathematical shape.

name: Paul Cohen
note: Cohen answers Gödel; forcing showed the other direction could not be settled from ZFC either.

name: Alain Chenciner
note: Chenciner and Montgomery share the proof; their variational argument turned a remarkable numerical orbit into an established periodic solution.

name: Ernő Rubik
note: I gave Rubik a place in the hall as a designer whose spatial puzzle became a finite group with a precise, reachable state space.

name: Pierre Deligne
note: Deligne closes the Weil conjectures; he completed a structure Grothendieck had imagined.

name: Carles Simó
note: Simó's numerical work widens the choreography families, where one elegant orbit opens into a much larger catalogue.

name: Paul Schechter
note: Schechter's 1976 function sits beside galaxy counts; its faint-end rise and bright-end cutoff remain a useful shared description.

name: Andrew Wiles
note: Wiles holds a closed page; his long pursuit joined elliptic curves to modular forms and changed what a proof could reach.

name: Richard Montgomery
note: Montgomery stands beside the figure eight's existence proof and the geometry of its choreography; the numerical discovery does not stand alone.

name: Thomas Hales
note: Hales's proof fills the packing page; he turned Kepler's intuition into a result that survived formal checking.

name: Richard Taylor
note: Taylor shares the repair beside Wiles; the fix that made the proof hold was shared work, not a footnote.

name: Grigori Perelman
note: Perelman enters the hall on his own terms; he carried Ricci flow through the singularities and declined the honors that followed.

name: Harald Helfgott
note: Helfgott closes weak Goldbach; his blend of analysis and careful computation settled a centuries-old question.

name: Christopher Moore
note: Moore's numerical search found the equal-mass figure eight in 1993, before its existence was proved variationally.

name: Daniel Kunkle
note: Kunkle and Cooperman proved in 2007 that 26 turns suffice, a distinct step before the exact diameter was known.

name: Gene Cooperman
note: Cooperman and Kunkle share the 26-move milestone, where search and computation first brought the upper bound close to twenty.

name: Herbert Kociemba
note: Kociemba joins the four-author proof of the exact diameter, with Rokicki, Davidson, and Dethridge.

name: John Dethridge
note: Dethridge stands among the four authors who proved that every legal cube position lies within twenty face turns of solved.

name: John Welborn
note: Welborn's 23- and 22-move results narrowed the gap beside Rokicki before the 20-move proof.

name: Kent Ford
note: Ford's spectrograph and measurements stand beside Rubin's analysis; the curve depended on patient instrumentation as much as on interpretation.

name: Michael Reid
note: Reid's 20-turn lower bound from the superflip set the floor that the later diameter proof had to meet.

name: Morley Davidson
note: I kept Davidson's contribution explicit in the 2010 computation that closed both bounds at twenty face turns.

name: Morwen Thistlethwaite
note: Thistlethwaite's subgroup chain runs beside the cube; it turns an enormous search into four disciplined reductions.

name: Tomas Rokicki
note: Rokicki spans the improving upper bounds and the final joint diameter proof, with each milestone's collaborators kept visible.
